name: NATO strap

card.summary: A single-piece nylon watch strap that threads behind the watch and lets you swap colours and styles cheaply to change how a watch looks.
card.note: Fit depends on the watch's lug width; the strap loops behind the case so the watch sits slightly higher on the wrist.

quick.overview:
The NATO strap is a one-piece nylon strap that passes through both spring bars of a watch and wraps around the wrist, including behind the case. It comes in solid colours and the striped patterns that grew out of regimental colours, and it can transform a watch from dressy to casual in a minute.

For appearance, it is a low-cost way to change a watch's look and match it to an outfit, since straps are interchangeable and available in many colours.
quick.how: The strap is threaded through the watch's spring bars, and the loose end is folded back into keepers and secured with a buckle. People keep several in different colours and swap them to suit clothes or the occasion. Because the strap runs under the case, it is also used by people who find metal bracelets irritating.
quick.risks: Few risks. The watch sits a little higher on the wrist because of the strap layer behind the case. Wikipedia notes that straps like this can keep metal off the skin, which can help people with contact dermatitis.

lead: The NATO strap is a one-piece nylon watch strap that runs through the watch's spring bars and around the wrist, including behind the case. The excess is folded back so it does not stick out.[1]

The design traces to a British Ministry of Defence specification: Defence Standard 66-47 describes a 20 mm nylon ribbon in Admiralty Grey and was introduced in 1973. The strap is also called the G10. Soldiers customised them with regimental colours, which produced the striped patterns the style is now known for.[1]

As a style item, it is an inexpensive way to change how a watch looks. A thicker-weave variant with heavier hardware is known as the Zulu strap, and related straps include Perlon and the elastic Marine Nationale.[1]

chain: Swap the watch onto a coloured or striped nylon strap
angle.text: A watch worn on a NATO strap looks different from the same watch on a bracelet or leather strap. Because the straps are inexpensive and swap in minutes, people use them to match colours to clothing and to dress a watch up or down.

paras: A NATO strap is a single piece of nylon that threads under the watch's spring bars and wraps behind the case, secured with a buckle. Hardware is typically metal, and straps come in plain colours and in the striped patterns associated with military regiments.[1]
The UK Ministry of Defence introduced the specification in 1973.[1] Regimental colours added by soldiers produced the stripes that later became a fashion staple.[1]

Wikipedia notes that NATO-style straps shield the skin from metal, which can help people with contact dermatitis, because the full wrap-around design differs from styles in which the case back touches the skin.[1]

timeline.event: UK Ministry of Defence introduces the nylon strap specification (DefStan 66-47).[1]
